pages.c01-p03: Understand that a computer system consists of a user interface, processes and data, and explain the factors that affect the choice of user interface

q.q: Which definition of a system matches the one used in systems development?
o: A computer program that accepts input, processes it and produces output for a single user
A set of independent programs that each carry out a separate task for an organisation
A collection of hardware devices connected together so that they can share data and resources
A set of interdependent components working together to achieve a stated purpose and satisfy an identified need
q.why: A system is defined by interdependent components, a defined purpose and a defined need; the other options miss one or more of these.

q.q: Which is NOT one of the three characteristics of a system given in the notes?
o: A graphical interface through which users interact
A defined purpose stating what it is for
A defined need that it satisfies
Components that depend on one another
q.why: The three characteristics are a defined purpose, a defined need and interdependent components; many systems have no graphical interface.

q.q: A council's recycling booking system is described as 'to let residents book recycling-centre visits online'. Which characteristic does this sentence describe?
o: Its defined purpose
Its sub-system interface
Its defined need
Its interdependent components
q.why: The purpose says what the system is for, usually in one sentence beginning 'to...'.

q.q: 'Queues at the recycling centre were causing traffic on the main road.' Which characteristic of the booking system does this describe?
o: Its decomposition into sub-systems
Its interdependent components
Its defined need
Its defined purpose
q.why: The need is the problem the system solves; the purpose is what the system is for.

q.q: In a recycling booking system, the gate barrier stops opening when the booking database goes offline. Which characteristic does this illustrate?
o: A defined purpose
A defined need
Independent sub-systems
Interdependent components
q.why: A fault in one component affecting another shows that the components are interdependent.

q.q: Why are large systems, such as those in a regional health trust, decomposed into sub-systems?
o: They are too complex to understand, build or maintain as one block
Each sub-system can then be built without any testing
Sub-systems no longer need to share data with one another
It removes the need to design interfaces between parts
q.why: Decomposition makes complex systems manageable; sub-systems still share data and interfaces must be designed carefully.

q.q: Which is a benefit of decomposing a large system into sub-systems?
o: The whole system needs only one development team
A sub-system can be replaced without rebuilding the whole system
Interfaces between parts no longer need to be designed
Changes in one sub-system can never affect another one
q.why: The notes list separate teams, replacement without rebuilding and easier fault-finding as benefits.

q.q: A health trust changes the format of its patient numbers in the patient administration sub-system. What is the main risk?
o: The patient administration sub-system becomes an independent system
Other sub-systems that use patient numbers may stop working correctly
The pharmacy sub-system will need a brand-new defined purpose
Decomposition will no longer be possible for the trust
q.why: A change to an interface in one sub-system can break others, so interfaces must be designed carefully.

q.q: Which list gives the five things every computer system must be able to do?
o: Collect, analyse, secure, back up and present data
Receive, process, store, verify and print data
Input, validate, sort, search and output data
Receive, process, store, present and communicate data
q.why: The five functions are receive, process, store, present and communicate.

q.q: A computer system can be described in terms of three elements. What are they?
o: Hardware, software and people
Input, process and output
Data, information and knowledge
Data, processes and a user interface
q.why: The model describes any computer system as data, processes and a user interface.

q.q: In a school cashless canteen, the fingerprint reader at the till is part of which element?
o: The communicate function
The user interface
The processes
The data
q.why: It is how users send data into the system, so it is part of the user interface.

q.q: In a school cashless canteen, 'deduct the cost of the meal from the pupil's balance' is an example of which element?
o: Data
The user interface
A process
Information
q.why: Processes are operations that manipulate data, such as deducting a cost.

q.q: In a school cashless canteen, which of these is an item of data?
o: Emailing a parent when the balance is low
Checking the balance before a sale
Each pupil's account balance
The parents' top-up app on a phone
q.why: The balance is a raw fact held by the system; the others are processes or interface.

q.q: Which of these is information rather than data?
o: 'Your balance is £14.20 – please top up before Friday'
Balance: 14.20
q.why: Information is processed data with context and meaning; the bare figures lack that context.

q.q: A wrong price is entered for a canteen meal, so every pupil's balance becomes wrong. Which element has caused the problem?
o: Processes
Data
User interface
Communication
q.why: Inaccurate data makes output unreliable even if processes and interface are fine.

q.q: The canteen system takes so long to calculate each sale that lunch queues grow. Which element is most likely at fault?
o: User interface
Processes
Data
Storage
q.why: Badly designed or inefficient processes make the system slower than necessary.

q.q: Which is NOT one of the five functions of a computer system?
o: Guarantee that the data entered is true
Present processed data to people as information
Communicate data to and from related sub-systems
Store data received and new data created
q.why: Systems can check data is sensible but cannot guarantee it is true.

q.q: Which three factors decide the choice of user interface?
o: The data, the processes and the information
The cost, the time and the user needs
The application, the environment and the users
The hardware, the software and the network
q.why: Mark schemes credit application, environment and users.

q.q: A GP receptionist enters many fields of patient detail all day. Why is a keyboard, mouse and form-based screen suitable?
o: Touchscreens are unable to send data to a database
Many fields of data are entered by trained staff
It is always the cheapest kind of interface to buy
Members of the public will be using it with no training
q.why: Application (many fields) and users (trained staff) justify a detailed interface.

q.q: A factory floor is extremely noisy. Which alert method would be least suitable?
o: Large on-screen alerts
Vibrating wristband alerts
Spoken audio alerts only
Flashing warning lights
q.why: The environment would drown out spoken alerts.

q.q: A self-service kiosk in a leisure centre will be used by members of the public with no training. Which interface design best suits these users?
o: Dense screens with keyboard shortcuts for speed
Many detailed form fields entered with keyboard and mouse
Large buttons, few steps and accessibility features
Command-line input with typed codes for each option
q.why: Public systems must be simple and intuitive with accessibility features.

q.q: Why is the user interface often decisive in whether a system succeeds?
o: It is often the only part of the system users ever see
It holds all of the system's data permanently
It is the most expensive part of the system to build
It carries out all of the system's calculations
q.why: The UI is the gateway to the system; poor usability means it is used badly or not at all.

q.q: A delivery app is used by drivers in a moving vehicle. Which factor most directly suggests voice control?
o: The cost
The environment
The application
The data volume
q.why: A moving vehicle is an environment issue: the driver cannot look away from the road.

q.q: A barcode scanner is chosen for a supermarket till rather than a keyboard. Which factor best justifies this?
o: The application needs many fields of detailed data entered
The application involves few inputs repeated very often
The users are untrained members of the public with disabilities
The environment is outdoors and the device must be rugged
q.why: Few inputs repeated often suit a scanner or touchscreen.

q.q: A pupil writes 'Use a touchscreen' as the whole answer to 'Explain the choice of interface'. Why does this score nothing?
o: It should have listed the three factors without a device
It should have named a keyboard and mouse instead
Touchscreens are never suitable interfaces for computer systems
It names a device without linking it to the application, environment or users
q.why: Answers are marked as factor plus justification pairs linked to the scenario.

q.q: Car parks now read number plates rather than issue paper tickets. What does this example illustrate?
o: User interfaces evolve as technology and needs change
Car parks have no need for a user interface
Number plate recognition is a defined purpose
Interfaces must never change once a system is live
q.why: Interfaces evolve with technology, e.g. cash to contactless or tickets to plate recognition.

q.q: A satnav app is used by voice while driving and by touch when parked. What does this show?
o: Some systems change interface during use to suit the environment
Voice interfaces have replaced touch interfaces entirely
Touch interfaces cannot be used in a car at all
The app has two separate defined purposes
q.why: The notes give this as an example of a system changing interface during use.

q.q: Whose needs must a successful system meet?
o: Only the organisation that pays for the system
Only the customers who buy the products
Both the organisation's and those of the individuals who use it
Only the developers who build and maintain it
q.why: There are usually two sets of needs: the organisation's and the individuals' (customers and staff).

q.q: Why must an online booking system meet the needs of individual customers as well as the company?
o: Customers are responsible for maintaining it
The law requires each customer to sign it off
Customers usually pay for the system's development
Customers who find it hard to use may book with a competitor
q.why: If users go elsewhere, the organisation loses income and the system fails its purpose.

q.q: Staff find a new rota system awkward and keep their own 'shadow' spreadsheet instead. What does this mainly show?
o: The system fully meets the needs of the individual staff
A system that ignores user needs can fail even if it works technically
Spreadsheets are always better than bespoke systems
The organisation's needs were met so the system succeeded
q.why: Workarounds show the system does not meet staff needs, wasting the investment.

q.q: Which is an organisation's need rather than an individual customer's need for a ferry booking system?
o: Receiving an instant booking confirmation
Handling high volumes of bookings efficiently and filling every sailing
Seeing clear prices before paying
Booking quickly at any time of day on a phone
q.why: The organisation wants volume, efficiency and full sailings; the others are individual needs.

q.q: A company wants to collect lots of marketing data at checkout, but customers want a short form. What is the analyst's role here?
o: Remove the checkout form so neither need applies
Always side with the customer because they use the system
Help the client strike the right balance between the conflicting needs
Always side with the company because it pays for the system
q.why: When needs conflict, the analyst must help the client balance them.

q.q: Where are most individual users' needs met or missed?
o: In the user interface
In the database design
In the payback period
In the project schedule
q.why: The notes state the UI is where most individual needs are met or missed.

q.q: Which answer would earn most credit for 'Explain why the booking site must be easy to use'?
o: Otherwise customers will book with a competitor, so the company loses income
It must be easy to use because ease of use is very important
Easy systems are usually more modern than harder ones
Customers like easy websites more than difficult websites
q.why: A strong answer links the need to a consequence for the organisation.

q.q: Why might a council need an automated billing system for collecting rates?
o: Individual householders asked for an online game
It wants to remove the need to store any records
It must bill every household, which cannot be handled efficiently one-to-one
Automated systems never need to comply with the law
q.why: Organisations need systems to fulfil purposes that could not otherwise be met efficiently, e.g. high volumes.

q.q: Which is the best definition of an information system?
o: Software that processes raw facts into reports for senior managers only
A database of records that is accessed through a web browser
People, procedures, hardware, software and data that collect, process, store and distribute information
Hardware and software that store data on a single computer for one user
q.why: An information system combines people, procedures, hardware, software and data.

q.q: Which is an internal reason for developing a new information system?
o: A competitor launches a mobile ordering app
Staff re-enter the same data on three different forms
Customers now expect 24/7 online access
New data protection legislation is passed
q.why: Duplicated data entry is a problem inside the organisation.

q.q: Which is an external reason for developing a new information system?
o: Managers need faster information for decisions
The business has grown beyond what the system can handle
The legacy system is unreliable and costly to maintain
HMRC introduces digital tax reporting requirements
q.why: New legislation comes from outside the organisation, so it is external.

q.q: What is a legacy system?
o: A newly installed system that replaced an old manual one
A system that is inherited when two firms merge together
An old system still in use that may be unreliable, unsupported or costly to maintain
A prototype that is kept as a record of the design
q.why: Legacy systems are outdated but still relied upon.

q.q: A change in data protection law forces a business to alter how its system works. How should this trigger be classified?
o: Neither, because legislation is not a reason for change
Internal, because the organisation changes its own system
External, even though the organisation must respond internally
Internal, because staff must change their working practices
q.why: A change in the law comes from outside, so it is external.

q.q: Which answer would earn most credit for 'Explain one reason a dental practice needs a new system'?
o: The practice wants to appear modern and up to date to its patients
Computers are generally better than paper for running a practice
A new computerised system would be much faster than the old one
The paper diary can be used by one receptionist at a time, so callers wait and some book elsewhere
q.why: It gives a specific problem and its consequence for the organisation.

q.q: Two companies merge and their customer systems must be combined. How is this trigger classified?
o: External
Internal
Legal
Schedule
q.why: A merger or reorganisation requiring systems to be combined is listed as an internal trigger.

q.q: Since 30 September 2026, which body has overseen data protection in the UK?
o: The Competition and Markets Authority
The Information Commissioner's Office
Ofcom
The Information Commission
q.why: The notes state the Information Commission (formerly the ICO) has overseen data protection since 30 September 2026.

q.q: Why is legislation described as a powerful trigger for a new system?
o: Compliance with the law is not optional
Legislation always reduces the cost of a system
Laws require all systems to be replaced every five years
New laws make old systems run more slowly
q.why: An organisation must comply, so a system that cannot meet the law may need replacing.

q.q: Where and when was the term 'software crisis' popularised?
o: At an IBM developers' conference in California, United States, in 1978
At the NATO Software Engineering Conference, Garmisch, Germany, October 1968
At the NATO Software Engineering Conference, Brussels, Belgium, October 1958
At a British Computer Society meeting in London, England, in 1968
q.why: The term was popularised at the NATO conference in Garmisch in October 1968.

q.q: What underlying problem led to the software crisis?
o: Too many specialist testers delayed every project
Hardware became too slow to run the software being written
Organisations stopped demanding new computer systems
Demand for large, complex systems grew faster than the ability to build software
q.why: Hardware improved and demand rose, but the ability to build software did not keep pace.

q.q: Which was a cause of the software crisis?
o: Development tools that were too advanced for programmers
Too many specialist testers checking each program
Little past experience of similar projects on which to base estimates
Users who only wanted very small, simple systems
q.why: With no history of similar projects, estimates were crude and wrong.

q.q: During the software crisis, imprecise methods for capturing requirements mainly led to…
o: too much documentation being produced
systems that did not do what users actually needed
faults being found early and cheaply corrected
deadlines being met but budgets being exceeded
q.why: Poor requirements capture meant the wrong system was built.

q.q: During the software crisis, the lack of tools to help find errors early mainly led to…
o: faults that were slow and expensive to locate and correct
more accurate time and cost estimates
cheaper maintenance once systems were live
software that was written faster than planned
q.why: Late discovery of faults made correction and maintenance costly.

q.q: Having no specialist testers or formal testing process during the software crisis mainly resulted in…
o: systems that exactly matched user requirements
low-quality, less robust software reaching users
crude and inaccurate cost estimates
projects finishing ahead of schedule
q.why: Without formal testing, poor-quality software reached users; inaccurate estimates came from lack of experience.

q.q: Which best defines software engineering?
o: Designing and repairing the hardware on which software will run
Testing completed software to find faults before it is released
Applying a disciplined, structured approach to the design, development and maintenance of software
Writing program code as quickly as possible to meet a tight deadline
q.why: Software engineering brings engineering discipline to all of software development.

q.q: Which was part of the response to the software crisis?
o: Writing software informally in small groups
Leaving testing to the users after installation
Formal life cycles such as the SDLC with defined stages
Removing client sign-off to speed projects up
q.why: Responses included life cycles, signed-off specifications, documentation standards, testing and project management.

q.q: An exam asks for the impact of the software crisis. Which answer best fits the notes?
o: Hardware became more expensive than software for most organisations
Software projects were cancelled because hardware was too slow
Software was late, over budget, unreliable and often failed to meet user requirements
Programmers were replaced by automated code generation tools
q.why: The overall impact was late, over-budget, unreliable software, sometimes abandoned.

q.q: What is a deliverable in the SDLC?
o: A working system delivered to the client at the end of the project
A list of tasks given to programmers at the start of development
A milestone date by which a stage of work must be completed
A document or product checked and signed off by the client before the next stage
q.why: Each stage has a deliverable signed off before the next begins.

q.q: Which deliverable is produced at the end of analysis?
o: The system (requirements) specification
The completed test plan and results
The feasibility report
The design specification
q.why: Analysis establishes and documents the requirements; a common mix-up is to place it in design.

q.q: Which is the correct order of SDLC stages?
o: Feasibility, analysis, design, development, testing, implementation
Analysis, feasibility, design, testing, development, implementation
Feasibility, design, analysis, development, implementation, testing
Analysis, design, feasibility, development, testing, implementation
q.why: The SDLC runs feasibility → analysis → design → development → testing → implementation → maintenance and evaluation.

q.q: At which SDLC stage is data converted, users trained and the system changed over?
o: Maintenance and evaluation
Implementation
Development
Testing
q.why: Implementation covers installing, converting data, training, changeover and handover.

q.q: What is the purpose of the design stage?
o: Plan how the new system will meet the requirements
Decide whether the project is possible and worthwhile
Check that the built system works correctly
Investigate the current system and establish the requirements
q.why: Design plans inputs, outputs, data, processes and a test plan to meet the requirements.

q.q: What is the difference between testing and evaluation?
o: Testing judges whether objectives were met; evaluation checks the code works
Testing is done by users; evaluation is done only by programmers
Testing happens after implementation; evaluation happens before design
Testing checks the system works; evaluation judges whether it met its objectives once in use
q.why: This is one of the classic mix-ups highlighted in the notes.

q.q: Why is the SDLC called a life cycle?
o: It is drawn as a circle so that it fits neatly on one page
The stages are repeated every week until the system is finished
Testing happens in a loop until no errors remain in the code
Evaluation and maintenance eventually show the need for a new system, starting a new study
q.why: When a system no longer meets needs, a new feasibility study begins.

q.q: Why are errors in requirements best found early?
o: Requirements cannot change once analysis has started
Clients are not allowed to change their minds later
Fixing them later means redesigning, recoding and retesting
Late errors are cheaper because more is known by then
q.why: The cost of correction rises at every stage.

q.q: What is the main weakness of a strict sequential life cycle?
o: It produces no documentation until the end
It does not include a testing stage
It has no point at which the client signs off work
It is inflexible when the client's requirements change late on
q.why: Going back to earlier stages is slow and expensive, which led to prototyping and Agile.

q.q: Which deliverable belongs to the maintenance and evaluation stage?
o: Post-implementation review
Design specification
Feasibility report
User guide
q.why: Maintenance and evaluation produces a maintenance log and post-implementation review; the user guide comes from implementation.

q.q: Which factor sets the scope of what must be built?
o: Time
Hardware
Cost
User needs
q.why: User needs define what the system must do.

q.q: A system must be live by the start of the tourist season. This is a…
o: time constraint
cost constraint
legal requirement
user-needs constraint
q.why: A fixed operational date is a time constraint.

q.q: A project's budget is cut part-way through. What is the most likely consequence?
o: The deadline moves earlier
No effect on the project
More features can be added
Fewer developers or a smaller system
q.why: Less money limits staff, hardware and scope.

q.q: In systems development, what is a constraint?
o: A stage in the life cycle
A limit the project must work within
A fault found during testing
A requirement the user has added late
q.why: User needs, time and cost each act as a constraint.

q.q: The client adds several new features but keeps the same deadline. What else is most likely to have to change?
o: Nothing, because the scope is unchanged
Cost, because more staff will be needed
Time, because the deadline will move earlier
User needs, because features were removed
q.why: Adding features increases time and cost; if time is fixed, cost must rise.

q.q: Why is cutting testing to meet a deadline described as a false economy?
o: Testing is the cheapest stage so cutting it saves little
Users always prefer systems that have not been tested
Faults found later by users are far more expensive to correct
Testing can only be done after the deadline anyway
q.why: This repeats a mistake from the software crisis.

q.q: Which answer would earn two marks for explaining the effect of cost on development?
o: Cost is one of the three factors affecting the development
The budget limits how many programmers can be employed, so fewer features can be built
Cost is the money spent by the organisation on the project
Cost is how much the whole system costs to build and run
q.why: You must explain the effect, not just name or define the factor.

q.q: A module would take a year to build, but the system must be live in six months. What should happen?
o: The module should be built with no extra cost
The module should be cut or delayed
More testing should be added to the module
The module should be built and the deadline ignored
q.why: Features that cannot be ready in time must be cut or delayed.

q.q: What is the main purpose of a feasibility study?
o: To establish the detailed requirements of the new system for the designers
To decide whether a proposed system is possible and worthwhile before money is committed
To check the finished system works correctly before it goes live
To plan the inputs, outputs and processes of the new system in detail
q.why: It ends with a recommendation to proceed, proceed with changes, or abandon.

q.q: What does TELOS stand for?
o: Technical, Economic, Legal, Operational, Schedule
Technical, Economic, Logical, Operational, Staffing
Technical, Efficient, Legal, Organisational, Social
Time, Economic, Legal, Operational, Security
q.why: TELOS is the five feasibility criteria.

q.q: Which feasibility criterion asks whether staff and customers will accept and use the system?
o: Schedule
Economic
Operational
Technical
q.why: Operational feasibility considers whether it works in practice with real people.

q.q: A system must comply with UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018. Which criterion covers this?
o: Economic
Legal
Technical
Operational
q.why: Compliance with legislation is legal feasibility.

q.q: A gym's facial-recognition system would need a network that can handle live video from four cameras. Which criterion does this concern?
o: Economic
Operational
Schedule
Technical
q.why: Whether the technology and network capacity exist is technical feasibility.

q.q: A new tax system must be working before a change in the law takes effect in April. Which criterion does this concern?
o: Schedule
Economic
Operational
Legal
q.why: Whether it can be delivered by a fixed deadline is schedule feasibility.

q.q: Reception staff have little IT experience and may resist a new system unless trained. Which criterion is this?
o: Economic
Technical
Legal
Operational
q.why: Staff attitudes and skills are operational; do not confuse with technical (does the technology work?).

q.q: Which alternatives should a feasibility study consider?
o: Only off-the-shelf packages, because bespoke systems cost too much
Only new systems, because doing nothing is never an option
Alternative solutions, including improving the current system or doing nothing
Only the single solution that the client has already chosen
q.why: A feasibility study compares alternatives, including doing nothing.

q.q: Which act would be considered under legal feasibility in Northern Ireland when checking disability discrimination duties?
o: Disability Discrimination Act 1995
Equality Act 2010
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
Computer Misuse Act 1990
q.why: In NI the disability discrimination duties come from the Disability Discrimination Act 1995.

q.q: Which is an intangible benefit?
o: Lower stock wastage
£6 000 a year saved in overtime
Reduced postage costs
Improved customer satisfaction
q.why: It is real but hard to give a money value.

q.q: Which is a tangible benefit?
o: Better management decisions
Improved reputation
Better staff morale
Fewer staff hours needed each week
q.why: Tangible benefits are measurable in money, such as saved staff hours.

q.q: Which is a one-off cost?
o: Licence renewal
Annual support contract
Printer ink and other consumables
Converting existing records to the new format
q.why: Data conversion happens once; the others are ongoing.

q.q: What is the payback period?
o: The time until the hardware must be replaced
The time until the system is fully developed
The time until cumulative benefits equal cumulative costs
The time until the first benefit is received
q.why: Payback is reached when the cumulative total reaches zero.

q.q: A system costs £20 000 to develop. It saves £9 000 a year and has running costs of £4 000 a year. What is the payback period?
o: 2.2 years
5 years
1.5 years
4 years
q.why: Net saving is £5 000 a year; £20 000 ÷ £5 000 = 4 years. 2.2 years forgets the running costs.

q.q: A system has a one-off cost of £30 000 and a net saving of £10 000 a year. Using a cumulative total that starts at –£30 000, in which year is payback reached?
o: Year 2
Year 4
Year 1
Year 3
q.why: Cumulative: –20 000 after year 1, –10 000 after year 2, 0 after year 3.

q.q: A system costs £12 000 one-off. Net benefits are £3 000 in year 1, £4 000 in year 2 and £5 000 in year 3. When is payback reached?
o: End of year 3
During year 2
End of year 2
End of year 4
q.why: Cumulative: –9 000, –5 000, then 0 at the end of year 3.

q.q: Why might a project go ahead even though its payback period is long?
o: Intangible benefits may tip the decision
Tangible benefits are ignored in the decision
The feasibility report never shows payback
Long payback periods always mean low costs
q.why: Intangible benefits like reputation may justify a project despite slow payback.

q.q: Who is the main audience of a feasibility report?
o: Senior managers or the client
Testers
Programmers
Customers
q.why: They use it to decide whether to commit money to the project.

q.q: Which section of a feasibility report states what the study was asked to investigate?
o: Justified recommendation
TELOS findings
Terms of reference
Description of the current system
q.why: The introduction and terms of reference set out the scope of the study.

q.q: In a payback calculation, a pupil makes an arithmetic slip but sets out a correct year-by-year table with a cumulative row. What is likely?
o: No marks, because the final figure is wrong
Marks only for the intangible benefits listed
Full marks, because the method is correct
Method marks can still be awarded
q.why: Method marks are often available even if a slip spoils the final figure.

q.q: What is the main role of the systems analyst?
o: Write and test the source code from the module specifications
Install the system and train the users at implementation
Plan, co-ordinate and financially control the project so it is delivered on time
Identify the user and data processing requirements of the new or modified system
q.why: The analyst finds out what the system must do.

q.q: Who produces the system specification?
o: Systems analyst
Programmer
Client
Project manager
q.why: Defining the specification is a core analyst duty.

q.q: Allocating staff, hardware and software to tasks is a duty of the…
o: end user
programmer
project manager
systems analyst
q.why: Resource allocation is project management.

q.q: Which is a programmer duty?
o: Reporting progress to the client
Interviewing the client's staff
Adding meaningful comments to code
Writing the feasibility report

Another programmer
The project manager
The systems analyst

A misunderstood requirement becomes very expensive to put right after coding
The analyst writes most of the program code

Identifying risks and monitoring progress

q.q: A programmer's module adds a yearly net saving of £10 000 to a cumulative total starting at –£30 000, increasing a year counter each time, until the total is no longer negative. What does it output?
o: Payback reached in year 2
Payback reached in year 3
Payback reached in year 4
Payback reached in year 0
q.why: After three loops the total reaches 0, which is not negative, so the loop stops with year = 3.

The feasibility report and cost–benefit analysis

Interview notes collected directly from users
